bac-u1-l3: Reading Why Do Children Leave School? Unit / ThemeUnit 1 · Education Level1st Bac Before you read Look at the pictures. What problem does the text talk about? ✚ image a long road to school ✚ image children working on a farm ✚ image bording house READING A social problem: school dropout The text Read it twice: once quickly, then carefully. [1] Fatima Zahra is fourteen. She lives in a small village in the mountains near Azilal. Two years ago, she left school. “I loved my teacher and I was good at maths,” she says, “but the middle school is fifteen kilometres from my house.” Her story is not unusual. Every year, thousands of Moroccan children drop out of school, especially in the countryside. [2] Why do they leave? Poverty is the main reason. Some families cannot pay for books, clothes or transport, so children work on farms or in shops to help their parents. Distance is another problem: some villages have no middle school, and the roads are bad in winter. [3] Girls are often the first victims. Some parents think a girl does not need a diploma, or they are afraid to let her travel alone. As a result, many girls stay at home and help with the housework. [4] Today, the government and local associations are trying to help. The Tayssir programme gives money to poor families when their children go to school. School buses and boarding houses for girls, called Dar Taliba, help them continue their studies. And Fatima Zahra has good news: next September, she is going back to school. “This time,” she smiles, “I won't stop!” A. Read quickly. Tick (✓) the best title for the text. bac-u1-l4: Grammar The Simple Past · My Grandfather's School Days Unit / ThemeUnit 1 · Education Level1st Bac Context Meet the grammar ✚ image a louh (wooden board) ✚ image a village school in the 1960s The text Read. Did Hajj Ahmed go to high school? Why? Underline the past verbs. My grandfather, Hajj Ahmed, was born in a small village near Ouarzazate in 1956. When he was five, he went to the msid, the village Quranic school. He didn't have books or notebooks. He wrote on a wooden board, the louh, and he learned the Quran by heart. At seven, he started primary school. The school was six kilometres from his house, so he walked there every morning with his brother. There were fifty pupils in one classroom! The teacher was very strict, but my grandfather loved him. In 1968, he passed his primary school exam. Did he go to high school? No, he didn't. His family was poor, so he stopped school and worked with his father on the farm. — Salma Form Focus on the form A. Find examples in the text. Then complete the table. The first line is an example. Affirmative Negative Question Short answers Regular verbs He walked to school. He didn't walk to school. Did he walk to school? Yes, he did. / No, he didn't. Irregular verbs Be (singular) Be (plural) Remember • Regular verbs: verb + -ed → walked, loved, studied, stopped. • Irregular verbs: learn them by heart → go → went, have → had, write → wrote. • Negative and questions: didn't / Did + base verb → He didn't have books. Did he go…? • Be: I / he / she / it was · you / we / they were. • Time markers: yesterday · last year · in 1968 · two years ago · when I was five. bac-u1-l5: Grammar Reflexive Pronouns · Life at Boarding School Unit / ThemeUnit 1 · Education Level1st Bac Context Meet the grammar ✚ image a boarding school in Ifrane ✚ image new students introduce themselves The text Read. How did Hind feel at the end of the week? Circle the words ending in -self / -selves. My first week at boarding school — by Hind, 15 Last September, I moved to a boarding school in Ifrane. The school itself is very old and beautiful. On the first day, the new students introduced themselves in the big hall. I was shy, so I only said, “I'm Hind. I'm from Azrou.” The headmistress smiled and said, “Welcome, girls! Enjoy yourselves!” My roommate, Aya, showed me the laundry room, so now I wash my clothes myself. On Wednesday, a boy in my class hurt himself in PE, but he was OK. Every evening, Aya and I made ourselves a cup of mint tea and did our homework. At the weekend, I phoned my mum. She asked, “Are you taking care of yourself?” I answered, “Yes, Mum. I'm proud of myself!” Form Focus on the form A. Find examples in the text. Then complete the table. The first line is an example. Singular Reflexive (-self) Plural Reflexive (-selves) Example from the text I myself we ourselves I'm proud of myself. you you he / she they it — — Remember • Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and the object are the same person: He hurt himself. • Singular → -self · plural → -selves. • by + myself = alone, without help: I did it by myself. • For emphasis: I wash my clothes myself. The school itself is old. • Common verbs: introduce · enjoy · hurt · cut · teach · take care of · be proud of. Teacher: Youssef Nejjar Grammar · page 1 Practice Use the grammar Grammar B. Predict: tick (✓) the ideas you expect to find in the text.Then read quickly and check. Families were bigger in the past. Teenagers had more freedom in the past than today. Neighbours helped each other in the past. There are new social problems in today's society. READING The text Read it twice: once quickly, then carefully. Then and Now — by Salma Alaoui [1] Last weekend, I interviewed my grandfather, Hajj Driss, for our school magazine. He is seventy-eight and he grew up in a small village near Ifrane. I asked him how society has changed since his childhood. His answers surprised me. [2] “When I was young, families were big,” he said. “My parents, my grandparents, my uncles and their children all lived in the same house, and nobody ate alone. Neighbours were like relatives: if a family had a problem, the whole village helped. Hospitality was a duty, and a traveller always found food and shelter in any home. Teenagers had little freedom. We obeyed our parents and started working very early. Life was hard, but we were rarely bored.” [3] When I asked him about today's society, he became serious. “Life is easier now. You have schools, hospitals and the internet. But people are lonelier. Families are smaller, and some young people spend more time with their phones than with their parents, and there is a real generation gap: parents and children often do not understand each other. In big cities I see homeless people in the streets, and many young graduates are jobless. In my time, divorce was rare; now it is more common.” [4] Finally, I asked him if he wanted to go back to the past. He smiled. “No, my dear. Every generation has its problems. Keep the good values of the past — respect, solidarity and tolerance — and use the new opportunities to build a better society.” While you read Understand the text Reading B. Skim the text. Teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, but many of them stay up late chatting or playing video games. Without enough sleep, your brain cannot concentrate in class, and your body becomes weak against colds and flu. ¶3 Second, eat a balanced diet. Start the day with a good breakfast, such as bread, eggs, fruit and a glass of milk. Avoid junk food and sugary drinks, which can lead to obesity and tooth decay. Drink at least six glasses of water a day: a lot of headaches are simply caused by dehydration. ¶4 Third, keep fit. You do not have to join a gym. Can We Still Save Our Coast? — by Anas Idrissi, school magazine ¶1 Every summer, thousands of families enjoy Morocco's beautiful beaches. But when they go home, they often leave something behind: plastic. Bottles, bags and food packaging end up in the sea, where they break into tiny pieces. Fish and turtles eat them, and the plastic finally comes back to us in our food. Some scientists warn that by 2050 there could be more plastic than fish in the oceans. ¶2 Plastic is not our only problem. In big cities like Casablanca, traffic and factories pollute the air, and many people suffer from breathing problems. At the same time, our country is facing long droughts. Rain is becoming rare, and we waste too much water in our homes and on our farms. ¶3 Fortunately, solutions exist. In 2016, Morocco banned plastic bags, and millions of shoppers now use cloth or paper bags instead. Our country has also become a leader in renewable energy: the Noor solar complex near Ouarzazate produces clean electricity for more than a million people. This means fewer fossil fuels and less pollution. ¶4 However, laws and power plants are not enough. Each of us can make a difference. We can recycle, carry a reusable water bottle, take shorter showers and walk or cycle instead of using the car. At Al Massira High School, the Green Club has already collected 300 kilos of rubbish from Agadir beach. If every school did the same, our coast would look very different. The planet is our only home, so let's protect it before it is too late. B. Skimming: match each paragraph with its main idea. The Ciné-Club: Our Favourite Escape Every Friday, forty students forget their homework and travel the world — without leaving Meknes. By Salma Bennani, 1st Bac · Al Kindi Magazine, March issue How it all started Three years ago, our English teacher, Mr. Karim Lahlou, borrowed an old projector and showed a documentary about the oceans in Room 12. Only six students came. Today, the Ciné-Club has more than forty members, and the screenings take place in the school hall every Friday at 4 p.m. More than films The club is not only about watching films. After each screening, members discuss the story, the characters and the music. Some students write reviews for this magazine, others design posters, and a small team is making its own short film about the old medina. “I used to be shy,” says Imane Chraibi, 17. “Now I give my opinion in front of everybody.” Last month, the members also visited a film studio in Ouarzazate, where they watched real actors at work. This month's hit In March, the club showed The Last Caravan, a Moroccan adventure film directed by Nadia Rami. It tells the story of a young guide from Merzouga who saves a lost caravan during a sandstorm. The hall was full, and many students said it was the best film of the year. Join us! Membership is free. All you need is curiosity and a little free time. If you are interested, see Mr. Lahlou in the English room before 25 April. New members can also suggest films for next term. Screens, Papers and Teenagers by Salma Idrissi, Our Voice school magazine 1 Last month, the media club at Ibn Rochd High School in Meknes asked 200 students a simple question: “How do you get the news?” The answers surprised our teachers. Only 12 students said they read a newspaper regularly, and most of them read it online, not on paper. 2 Television is still popular. About 45% of the students watch the evening news bulletin with their families, especially when there is a big football match or an important national event. However, the most popular source of information is the smartphone. Seven students out of ten follow the news on social media or on news websites every day. 3 This change worries some people. Anyone can post a story, and a false story can travel around the world in minutes.” He advises students to check the source of every piece of news and to compare two or three websites before sharing it. 4 The survey also showed that teenagers want to take part in the media, not only consume it. On that evening, we all gather at my grandparents' house in a small village near Tiznit to welcome Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year. For a long time, Yennayer was only a family and village celebration, but since 2024 it has been an official national holiday in Morocco. 5 For me, Yennayer is more than a party. Al-Qarawiyyin: Twelve Centuries of Learning ¶1 In the narrow streets of the old medina of Fez stands a building that has welcomed students for more than eleven centuries. Al-Qarawiyyin is not only a mosque; it is also one of the oldest places of learning in the world, and its story began with a woman. ¶2 In the ninth century, Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a rich merchant from Kairouan, inherited a large fortune from her father. Instead of keeping the money for herself, she decided to build a mosque for her community. The work started in 859, and the mosque soon became a meeting place for scholars. ¶3 Over the next centuries, Al-Qarawiyyin grew into a great university. Students travelled from Africa, Al-Andalus and even Europe to study religion, grammar, mathematics, medicine and astronomy. Many famous scholars, such as the historian Ibn Khaldun, are connected with its long history. ¶4 The mosque's library is one of the oldest in the world. It keeps thousands of precious manuscripts, including very old copies of the Quran and books on medicine and law. For many years, the building suffered from humidity and cracks. In 2016, after a long restoration led by the Moroccan architect Aziza Chaouni, the library was reopened. ¶5 Today, Al-Qarawiyyin is part of the medina of Fez, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981. It reminds us that our heritage is not only buildings and arts; it is also knowledge passed down from one generation to the next. Protecting places like this is a duty for all of us. Which rights do the students talk about? Every year on 10 December, the Dignity Club at Al Massira High School in Beni Mellal celebrates Human Rights Day. This year, our supervisor, Ms. Leila Benali, reminded us that all people are born free and equal in dignity and rights. We made posters about freedom of speech, the right to education and gender equality. Anas presented a report on child labour: thousands of children work in shops and fields instead of going to school. Khadija spoke about discrimination against disabled people and refugees. Mehdi showed that poverty and illiteracy often go together. At the end, we all promised to respect others, to defend the weakest and to fight injustice wherever we see it. Rights in Action: Four Stories from Our Region ¶1 Every Wednesday afternoon, the members of the Dignity Club at Al Massira High School in Beni Mellal meet to turn ideas into action. Last month, their supervisor, Ms. Leila Benali, asked them to look for real human rights stories in their region. The students came back with four stories. ¶2 Nadia is thirteen and lives in a small village near Azilal. Every morning, she walks eleven kilometres to the nearest middle school. In winter, snow often closes the road, so she misses classes for days. Three of her friends have already dropped out. “I wish the school were closer,” she told Salma. ¶3 In the old medina, Hamza met Omar, a twelve-year-old boy who repairs shoes in his uncle's shop instead of going to school. He earns forty dirhams a week for his family. Hamza learnt that child labour still keeps thousands of Moroccan children away from the classroom. ¶4 Imane interviewed Mr. Karim Alaoui, a history teacher who has used a wheelchair since a car accident in 2015. He explained that many public buildings still have no ramps or lifts. “Being disabled is not the problem; the problem is a city that forgets us,” he said. ¶5 Finally, Khadija visited a women's cooperative in Fkih Ben Salah, where thirty women attend a literacy class three times a week. Fatima, 52, wrote her name for the first time last spring. “Now I can read my children's school reports,” she said proudly. The club will present the four stories on Human Rights Day, 10 December. bac-u9-l6: Writing A formal letter: asking for help Unit / ThemeUnit 9 - Human Rights Level1st Bac Model Read Salma's letter to the commune council ✚ image A snowy road near Azilal ✚ image A school bus The model letter Who is writing? To whom? Why? Dignity Club, Al Massira High School Avenue Hassan II, Beni Mellal 15 November 2026 The President of the Commune Council Azilal Subject: A school bus for the pupils of Aït Ouchen Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing on behalf of the Dignity Club of Al Massira High School to ask for your help with a serious problem in the village of Aït Ouchen. Every day, many pupils walk more than ten kilometres to the nearest middle school. In winter, snow closes the road and they miss classes for days. As a result, several girls have already dropped out of school. We would be grateful if the council could provide a school bus for these children. In addition, we would like to suggest a small boarding house for girls near the school. Thank you for your attention. I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, Salma Idrissi Salma Idrissi, President of the Dignity Club A. READING The text Don't read every word: look for numbers, names, days and times. Dear Yassine, How are you? I'm writing to tell you about my new school. I'm now a Common Core student at Ibn Rochd High School in Meknes. It's a big school with 1,200 students and 65 teachers! From Job Seeker to Shop Owner [1] Kawtar Alami is twenty-six and lives in Safi. Three years ago, she lost her job when the fish factory closed. She was unemployed for a long time. Every morning, she looked for work in the newspapers and on the Internet, but she found nothing. [2] One day, her uncle gave her an idea: “You can cook very well. Why don't you sell your cakes?” Kawtar had some savings, but they weren't enough, so she got a small loan from a bank. With the money, she rented a tiny shop near the market and bought an oven. [3] At first, she had very few customers and she barely earned enough to pay the rent. But her cakes were delicious and cheap, and people soon came back for more. Today, Kawtar's shop is busy every day.
